newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan reports attack, Bashir visits front.
newsitem.headline: Sudan reports attack, Bashir visits front.

text.p: Sudan reported on Friday an attack on government troops on the northeastern front, the first in that area for more than a week.
Information Minister al-Tayeb Ibrahim Khair, quoted in the government newspaper al-Sudan al-Hadith, blamed the attack on Eritrean forces and said the army had beaten them off.

"The armed forces repelled an attempt by Eritrean forces to attack the border area between Gadamit and Togan, in the northeast of Kassala state, in which they sustained huge losses and a quantity of weapons and ammunition was seized," he said.
But Brigadier Khair then added that the casualty toll on the Eritrean side was one killed and several wounded. The newspaper did not say when the fighting took place.
Eritrea says it has nothing to do with the fighting and Sudanese rebels who have training camps inside Eritrea say they are responsible for the attacks, which began early last week.
There have been no independent accounts of the fighting in eastern Sudan and it is difficult to assess the value of the versions put out by the conflicting parties.

State radio said later that President Omar Hassan al-Bashir visited on Friday the southeastern town of Damazin, where government forces have been massing for a counterattack on what they say are invading Ethiopian forces.
"On arrival General Bashir held a meeting with the command of the 4th Infantry Brigade and the latest developments in the east were reviewed," the radio added.
The rebels have said they want to take Damazin, site of the hydroelectricity plant which supplies most of Khartoum's power, but their advance seems to have lost momentum.
In an interview published on Friday, President Bashir said forces were getting ready to "liberate" eastern Sudan from invading Ethiopian and Eritrean forces.

"The situation now is as follows: the initial attack from the Ethiopian and Eritrean forces has been contained, and our forces have stopped the advance of the enemy forces," Bashir told the leftwing Beirut daily as-Safir.
"Now they are getting ready, after grouping, to push to liberate the land...every inch of the land."
Bashir said a new front may be opened with Uganda but Khartoum would not move unless Uganda attacked first.

"We do not rule out opening a front with Uganda, especially after the leaders of these three countries (Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda) met in London last Thursday to coordinate against Sudan," Bashir said.
"There are forces mobilised on the Ugandan side of the border, but we will not move against Uganda unless it begins with aggression," Bashir added.
Another Sudanese newspaper, privately owned Alwan, said the rebel force based in Eritrea was so small that it posed no threat to the Sudanese army.
It quoted al-Awad Mahjoub, a defector from the oppostion, as saying that the rebel force, including the southerners of the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), amounted to 2,744 men.
He broke this down into SPLA 2,000, the Democratic Unionist Party 96, the Umma Party 40, Colonel Abdel Aziz Khaled's force 600 and General Fatih Ahmed Ali's force eight.
General Ali was commander in chief of the army when Bashir seized power in a military coup in 1989. Colonel Khaled is another defector from the army.
